newSourceLead.scope: Laboratory ethanol leaf extraction in an animal experiment; not a validated human recipe.
newSourceLead.reason: Separate source-quality and taxonomic review needed. No clinical or household preparation cleared.

limitations: All fifty candidates are research records, not complete reviewed import manifests.
Food descriptions, traditional reports, manufacturing and laboratory processing are not validated home treatment instructions.
All preparation references resolve to recorded sources. Source quality/freshness for every website was not revalidated this turn.
All-state comparison used names, queued synonyms, reviewed modern-name proposals and stored local aliases; it is not exhaustive taxonomic deduplication or a concurrency guarantee.
Cloudinary status/type/bytes/hash were rechecked. Full decoding, visual review and individual license verification were not repeated; their prior evidence remains in the original ledgers.
Nonblank live fields and source presence do not establish clinical validity.
No live AI answer or vector-only retrieval was retested in this audit. Three live embeddings are missing.
The separate twenty-existing-herb preparation update is already live; its local Dr. Ai dosage-context fix is not deployed by this audit.

preparation.part: Fruit
preparation.description: Culinary use, not treatment: duhat fruits are eaten fresh or processed into juice, sauces, jams and preserves. The source supplies no diabetes-treatment recipe.

preparation.part: Fruit pulp
preparation.description: Culinary use, not treatment: the tart pulp is used as a flavouring in curries, chutneys, jams, confectionery and beverages. No medicinal laxative dose or timed recipe is established.

preparation.part: Fruit flesh, excluding seeds
preparation.description: Culinary use, not treatment: mature fruit is eaten fresh or added to smoothies and desserts. Seeds must be removed before serving; the source identifies them as toxic when swallowed.

preparation.part: Fruit kernels, not leaf or bark
preparation.description: Food preparation only, not treatment: a published study sun-dried ripe fruits for one week, extracted kernels with a nutcracker, then roasted whole kernels with or without salt. It supplies no roasting temperature or duration. This describes kernel-food processing, not a validated medicinal preparation or treatment dose.

preparation.part: Flowers, not roots or seeds
preparation.description: Culinary use, not treatment: flowers supply an edible blue colour extract used in traditional Malay pastries. The reviewed source gives no extraction time, ratio or therapeutic flower-tea regimen.

preparation.part: Fruit flesh
preparation.description: Culinary use, not treatment: the edible ripe fruit has juicy yellow flesh. The reviewed page does not specify a cooking recipe; do not manufacture a leaf or bark decoction from its list of folk claims.

preparation.part: Whitish fruit pulp, not seeds
preparation.description: Culinary use, not treatment: the whitish pulp is eaten fresh or made into marmalade and candy. Medicinal bark and root instructions are not cleared by this food description.

preparation.part: Fruit flesh only in this proposed description
preparation.description: Culinary use, not treatment: papaya fruit is eaten, made into jellies or preserves, or cooked as a vegetable. This food description does not establish dengue treatment or a latex preparation.

preparation.part: Edible fruit pulp surrounding seeds
preparation.description: Culinary use, not treatment: the fruit pulp is eaten fresh or processed into juice, jellies and syrups. This does not establish a root-bark worm treatment.

preparation.part: Fruit flesh, not seed kernels or sap
preparation.description: Culinary use, not treatment: edible fruit is eaten fresh or used in desserts. The same source flags irritating sap and toxic seed ingestion, so no seed preparation is included.

preparation.part: Leaves and seeds
preparation.description: Culinary use, not treatment: mustard leaves are eaten in salads or cooked; seeds are used in curries and pickles. The source does not supply cooking times or medicinal quantities.

preparation.part: Cultivated taproot and leafy tops
preparation.description: Culinary use, not treatment: the swollen taproot is peeled, cut into small pieces and cooked in soups or meat dishes. The leafy tops may be stir-fried as a vegetable.

preparation.part: Leaves, young shoots and flower buds
preparation.description: Culinary use, not treatment: leaves and young shoots are consumed as vegetables; flower buds are added to salads. The reviewed modern source supplies no medicinal preparation quantities.

preparation.part: Seeds and surrounding fruit pulp
preparation.description: Food-processing overview, not treatment: seeds undergo fermentation and drying, then roasting, crushing, grinding and pressing to make chocolate products or cocoa butter. The surrounding pulp is eaten or processed into desserts. This is not a validated home fermentation protocol.

preparation.part: Leaves in the historical external report; seeds for allergen caution
preparation.description: Historical description only: the book reports sesame-leaf poultices. This is not recommended as a home treatment; medicinal preparation instructions remain withheld.

preparation.part: Coconut flesh
preparation.description: Culinary use, not treatment: coconut flesh is shredded for desiccated coconut or squeezed to obtain coconut milk. Coconut milk is an ingredient in curries and desserts; oil is also extracted from the flesh. Coconut milk is not the liquid naturally inside the fruit.

preparation.part: Corn silk (stigma), not tassel, grain or stalk
preparation.description: A draft EMA monograph describes cut corn silk as an oral herbal tea prepared by infusion or decoction. It addresses traditional use, not well-established clinical efficacy. No recipe or human dose is cleared here, and the book's tassel preparation is not substituted for corn silk.

preparation.part: Juicy stem (culm)
preparation.description: Food-processing overview, not treatment: juice is extracted from the soft tissue of sugarcane stems and processed into sugar or syrup. No medicinal heating time, dose or cough treatment is supplied.

preparation.part: Fennel material in a shared historical fennel/coriander discussion
preparation.description: Historical description only: the shared fennel and coriander passage mentions infusions and other extracts. It does not clear a modern, variety-specific preparation or human dose for this queue record.

preparation.part: Fruits (peppercorns)
preparation.description: Culinary use, not treatment: dried pepper fruits are used as food seasoning. NParks describes unripe fruits turning black when dried. No medicinal quantity or malaria regimen is supplied.

preparation.part: Leaves
preparation.description: Food preparation only, not treatment: fresh or dried common-basil leaves flavour tomato dishes; fresh leaves can be blended with other ingredients into pesto. The source supplies no complete ingredient ratios, cooking duration or medicinal regimen.

preparation.part: Leaves
preparation.description: Reported food use only, not treatment: a chemical-analysis paper describes Ocimum gratissimum leaves in Nigerian soups and salads as flavouring. Its background supplies no reproducible household recipe, ingredient amount or cooking time; laboratory extracts and handling are not food instructions.

preparation.part: Leaves
preparation.description: Food preparation only, not treatment: holy-basil leaves flavour salads and dishes containing fruit, fish or chicken. The selected food paragraph provides no ingredient amount or cooking time and does not validate a therapeutic tea regimen.

preparation.part: Leaves, not essential oil
preparation.description: Food preparation only, not treatment: rosemary leaves are used as a culinary dressing or to flavour smoked or roasted meat. No ingredient ratio, cooking time or medicinal dose is supplied; leaf seasoning is not essential-oil ingestion.

preparation.part: Unopened white flowers
preparation.description: Food preparation only, not treatment: the source describes unopened white flowers in the Philippines with stamen and calyx removed, then steamed or cooked in soups and stews. No amount or cooking duration is specified. This does not validate root, bark, leaf-tea or eye-drop remedies.

preparation.part: Young leaves, not seeds or bark
preparation.description: Food preparation only, not treatment: young leaves are cooked with fish or meat to flavour soup. The reviewed source provides no leaf quantity, cooking time or medicinal dose. Its separate seed-composition notes do not establish a seed-food recipe.

preparation.part: Seeds in laboratory flour processing
preparation.description: Laboratory food-processing description, not a home recipe or treatment: a Parkia timoriana study cut and rinsed seeds, soaked them in distilled water for 12 hours and cooked them before freeze-drying and milling to flour. The reviewed subsection does not specify the numeric cooking time. No household protocol or medicinal dose is cleared.

preparation.part: Young seeds
preparation.description: Food preparation only, not treatment: young translucent seeds, called attap chee, are boiled in sugar syrup and added to desserts. The source specifies no syrup ratio or boiling duration. This seed-food description does not clear sap fermentation or flower-sheath tea as medicinal preparations.

preparation.part: Young non-bitter fruit, not medicinal juice
preparation.description: Food preparation only, not treatment: young bottle-gourd fruit is described as boiled or used in stews, without a specified cooking time or ingredient amount. Discard bitter fruit and do not consume bitter juice. This food description is not a medicinal juice recipe or evidence that cooking clears toxicity.

preparation.part: Immature edible fruit, not mature sponge
preparation.description: Food preparation only, not treatment: young smooth-loofah fruit is fried, stewed, boiled or steamed as a vegetable. No quantity or cooking duration is given. Mature fibrous fruit is not the same food part, and a raw-use statement for sweet cultivars must not be generalized to all plants.

preparation.part: Not established for the exact species
preparation.description: The reviewed Gardenwise paragraph describes flowers under the genus Ixora but does not identify Ixora coccinea. No exact-species preparation method was established in this review; the lead is not treatment guidance.

preparation.part: Flowers of Jasminum sambac cv. bifoliatum used to scent Camellia sinensis tea
preparation.description: A primary tea study mixed opened flowers of Jasminum sambac cv. bifoliatum with prepared green tea in controlled scenting rounds, separated spent flowers and dried the tea between rounds. This manufacturing description is not a home recipe or treatment.

preparation.part: Ripe fruit flesh identified as edible; processing not established
preparation.description: NParks identifies edible yellow flesh around the seeds of ripe Mimusops elengi fruit. It supplies no preparation process, so no raw-serving, seed-oil, drying or cooking method is added. This edible-part description is not treatment guidance.

preparation.part: Young leaves reported as a vegetable; processing not established
preparation.description: NParks reports young Hibiscus tiliaceus leaves eaten as a vegetable but gives no cooking method. No boiling duration or roselle-style tea is supplied. This food-use statement is not treatment guidance.

preparation.part: Young flower buds and leaves
preparation.description: World Agroforestry reports young flower buds and leaves of Thespesia populnea eaten uncooked or fried using butter. No cooking duration or ingredient ratio is supplied. This culinary description is not treatment guidance.

preparation.part: Leaves, flowers and young fruits; seed oil excluded
preparation.description: PROTA describes Ceiba pentandra leaves, flowers and young fruits cooked into sauces. Its caution against culinary seed oil and reported digestive upset from seeds remain attached; seed and oil preparations are excluded. This culinary description is not treatment guidance.

preparation.part: Dried seeds used for a laboratory methanol extract
preparation.description: Alam and colleagues prepared an experimental extract from ground dried Sterculia foetida seeds using methanol maceration followed by rotary evaporation. This is laboratory processing, not a home recipe or treatment; no seed meal or cooking method is cleared.

preparation.part: Fruit; not root or bark
preparation.description: World Agroforestry describes Ziziphus mauritiana fruit consumed fresh or dried, processed into pickles, or macerated in water for a beverage. Ratios and processing times are not given. This culinary description is not treatment guidance.

preparation.part: Heartwood used for laboratory solvent extraction
preparation.description: Chen and colleagues extracted authenticated Pterocarpus indicus heartwood using ethanol soaking and heated reflux, then solvent fractionation and freeze-drying, for a rat study. This laboratory description is not a home recipe or treatment; it does not establish a human regimen.

preparation.part: Dried seeds (coffee beans), not leaves
preparation.description: World Agroforestry describes dried Coffea arabica seeds being roasted, milled and brewed into a beverage. The paragraph provides no brewing ratio or roasting duration. This seed-beverage description is not treatment guidance.

preparation.part: Fruit; no juice regimen
preparation.description: NParks reports green Averrhoa bilimbi fruit made into a relish in Suriname, without a full processing method. A human case report documents oxalate kidney injury after fruit juice and leaves cooking's effect on toxicity unresolved. This held food description is not treatment guidance.

preparation.part: Fruit; juice and medicinal regimens excluded
preparation.description: NParks describes Averrhoa carambola fruit in salads and preserves. A primary case series records oxalate-associated acute kidney injury after starfruit intake. The food description remains held for renal safety review and is not treatment guidance.

preparation.part: Fleshy cashew apple, not nut shell or seed oil
preparation.description: NParks describes the fleshy Anacardium occidentale cashew apple eaten fresh, included in fruit salads or preserved as jam. This does not supply nut-shell processing, roasting, fermentation or oil instructions. The culinary description is not treatment guidance.

preparation.part: Unripe fruit in a reported Thai traditional preparation
preparation.description: PROSEA reports a Thai traditional infusion or decoction using dried, thinly sliced unripe Morinda citrifolia fruit. This is a traditional-use description, not treatment guidance or clinical approval. Potassium, medication and liver-report uncertainties remain attached.

preparation.part: Leaves in reported seasoning use; no validated amount
preparation.description: PROSEA reports Oxalis corniculata leaves added to food as seasoning and warns that larger amounts can be toxic due to oxalates. It gives no safe amount or cooking controls. This held food-use report is not treatment guidance.

preparation.part: Bitter-orange fruit for marmalade, not concentrated extract or essential oil
preparation.description: The Dutch Botanical Gardens Association describes bitter-orange fruit used to make marmalade. No sugar ratio, boiling duration or canning process is supplied. This food description is not treatment guidance and must not be extended to concentrated supplements or essential oil ingestion.

preparation.part: No preparation adopted
preparation.description: The retrieved Magnolia champaca study has inconsistent retraction-link metadata: its linked notice concerns a different paper. The source is quarantined and no method is adopted. This unresolved research gap is not treatment guidance and is not a confirmed retraction finding.

preparation.part: Combined leaves, twigs and roots in a laboratory extract
preparation.description: A primary Abutilon indicum study dried and powdered combined leaves, twigs and roots, boiled the material in distilled water, freeze-dried the extract and prepared solvent fractions for preclinical experiments. This laboratory description is not a home recipe or treatment.

preparation.part: Seed in reported coffee flavouring; essential oil excluded
preparation.description: PROSEA reports Abelmoschus moschatus seeds used to flavour coffee, without specifying processing or a food-grade quantity. This is a reported food use, not a complete recipe or treatment guidance. Oil, perfume, incense and tobacco preparation are excluded.

preparation.part: Industrial dehydrated leaf/stem mash in analytical tea bags
preparation.description: A primary analytical study included Ayapana triplinervis industrial leaf/stem mash, prepared water infusions and decoctions, removed the tea bags and froze the samples for chemical and cell testing. This laboratory description is not a home recipe or treatment.
